title: MA9-00757
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX, is a citizen of El Salvador. Ms. XXXXXXX is alleging that she is a "Convention refugee" and a "person in need of protection" under section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
The claimant alleged that she met her future husband when she was 14 years old and that she went to live with him without her parents' permission.
He started to beat her that same year. She stayed with him because she had no other support.
She stated that, in 2002, since her husband is a Canadian citizen, he decided to come here to live; she followed him.
They stayed in Mexico for one and a half years in order to save up enough money to continue their trip.

When she arrived in the United States, she was detained in Arizona because she was a minor. She then met up with her spouse again in Los Angeles. They then went to live in Boston, where her son was born on XXXXXXX, 2004. They were married on XXXXX, 2005, and then came to Canada.
They were driven to the Canadian border, and she entered on XXXXXXX, 2005, with a temporary authorization, since she was the spouse of a Canadian citizen.
They lived with her husband's mother, but her husband went out often, used drugs and abused her. One day, he left for a month with another woman and no longer looked after her and her son.

Another day, he beat her badly. She went to a CLSC. He broke a glass door with her head and beat her with an electrical cable. She stated that she did not call the police because she was afraid and that she did not go to the women's shelter because she was told that it was like a prison and she did not need care.

In XXXXX 2008, her husband tried to beat her and she had to leave without her child. He then refused to let her see him. She finally ended up at a women's shelter with her child, and she found out that he did not have the right to forbid her from seeing her child.
She found out that she had received a deportation letter, but she did not know what her status was. She was afraid of returning to her country.
She claimed refugee protection in XXXXX 2008-three years after she arrived in Canada.
Having analyzed the documentary and testimonial evidence, the panel is of the opinion that the claimant is not a "Convention refugee" or a "person in need of protection". ANALYSIS Identity

Given the documents submitted as evidence,1 namely, the photocopies of her passport, which was valid from XXXXXX, 2005, to XXXXXX, 2010, and of her birth certificate, which is in her possession, the panel is satisfied as to the claimant's identity. Credibility
The claimant's testimony was not credible regarding her alleged fears should she return to El Salvador.

During her testimony, the claimant explained that she met her spouse, XXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXXX, in El Salvador when he was there on vacation. He is a Canadian citizen but was born in El Salvador. He allegedly went to the United States with his parents when he was around two years old and came to Canada later. She started living with him when she was 14 and he was 26. Sometime around 2003, they decided to come to Canada. She allegedly followed him to Mexico. He allegedly left her there for her to cross the border while he supposedly waited for her in the United States. After arriving in that country, she met her spouse in Los Angeles and gave birth to their son in Boston on XXXXXXX, 2004. They were married on XXXXX, 2005, before coming to Canada.

The panel is surprised that she stayed in the United States for 14 months, from XXXX 2004 to XXXXXXX 2005, without attempting to claim asylum. Her explanations on that topic are vague. She stated that she had a disagreement with her parents when she was in El Salvador because of her choice of spouse, and that she did not claim asylum in the United States, even though the entire family lives there, because she wanted to follow her husband, who is Canadian and therefore wanted to go to Canada.

Given the claimant's young age at the time and the possibility that she was abused, as she alleged, the panel accepts her explanations for not claiming asylum in the United States because she was following her spouse, who later became her husband, and because, since he is Canadian, she was considering coming to Canada, her husband's country of residence.

However, the panel wants to understand why the claimant waited three years to claim refugee protection in Canada. In fact, she entered Canada on XXXXXXX, 2005, with a temporary permit because she is married to a Canadian. She explained that he told her that he would apply to sponsor her, but that having lived under the yoke of her violent ex-husband for many years, she did not check her status at the time. Her spouse supposedly became more violent after they arrived in Canada. Allegedly, he was often away, used drugs and hit her often. On one of these occasions, he allegedly shoved her hard against a door and hit her on the legs and in the face. She allegedly bled and went to see a doctor at the CLSC, but she did not submit any documents on this subject. Questioned as to why she did not submit any documents from the CLSC, the claimant replied that she did not know that, that she did not know that she was supposed to do that. The date of this incident is difficult to establish. She replied that it happened before she left the house, around XXXXXXX 2008. However, the claimant mentioned at one point that she went to the CLSC a number of times. Once again, the dates of the visits are vague. She stated that her first visit occurred during the same month she left the house and then stated that it was in XXXXXXX 2008. She later stated that it started around 2007.
The failure to submit evidence to support the fact that she went to the CLSC, as well as the contradictions regarding the incidents that took place, surprises the panel.

The panel is surprised by the alleged visits to the CLSC and to the doctor and, consequently, by the allegations of domestic violence that she experienced. In fact, she was often confused in her answers, but in particular, she did not submit any documents from the CLSC to show that she had four or five interviews, as alleged, and received treatment. Furthermore, she provided no real explanation for this. She has, however, been in Quebec for three years and is being assisted by several lawyers, for, among other things, her divorce and her refugee protection claim.

In addition, it was only after the deportation order was issued on XXXXXXX, 2008, that the claimant took certain steps, including leaving her husband in XXXXXX 2008 and claiming refugee protection in XXXXXXX 2008. She went to a shelter for battered women on XXXXXXX, 2008, and started divorce proceedings on XXXXXXX, 2008. Her divorce was finalized on XXXXX, 2010-all of that because her spouse had become increasingly violent.

However, the panel took into account the other documents submitted. In addition to her Personal Information Form, the claimant submitted four documents to corroborate these allegations: a motion to institute divorce proceedings,2 her divorce decree,3 a court order issued against her spouse,4 and her removal order.5 The panel also took into account a document seized by Immigration Canada when the refugee protection claim was made: a letter from the XXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX6 dated XXXXXXXX, 2008, which confirms that the claimant started staying at this shelter with her son on XXXXXXXX, 2008, and was still living there as of XXXXXXXX, 2008.

The panel accepts the claimant's allegations that she was a victim of domestic violence, even though she never called the police-she was scared-and even though she did not submit any medical documents on this subject; because victims of domestic violence can experience difficulties testifying7 and have memory lapses, it is possible that the claimant, who is a young woman (born in 1987), would have some problems organizing her thoughts and gathering the documents required to support her testimony.

Consequently, the panel considers the claimant's explanations regarding her delay in claiming refugee protection to be reasonable, given that she was a victim of domestic violence and that she was only 14 when she met this man who is 12 years her senior and that she endured living under his control and had little contact outside of her home.

The panel wants to know what the claimant could fear should she return to El Salvador, since her spouse lives in Canada and is Canadian. The claimant stated that if she returned to El Salvador, her former spouse could return to El Salvador at any time to beat her or even kill her, as she alleged at the hearing, because he has a Canadian passport and because there is no protection there.

Also, the claimant never explained why her former spouse would want to return to El Salvador to find her. He was on holidays when she met him; he was XXXXXXX on a team, and they had no fixed address, as they both lived at different addresses, as stated at the hearing. The claimant also stated that her former spouse's entire family is in Canada. His grandmother is his only relative in El Salvador.
Therefore, the claimant's former spouse has little reason to return to El Salvador. He obviously does not have a residence there, and all of his family is in Canada, except for his grandmother.

The claimant, however, is the mother of a child who has been acknowledged by the father, which could constitute a reason for trying to find his former spouse in El Salvador if she were to leave Canada with the child. However, the father has applied for Canadian citizenship for his son, since he is the son of a Canadian. Given that the child's custody has not been stipulated in the divorce documents and that her son has Canadian citizenship, the panel is of the opinion that there is little chance that the claimant would leave the country with her son.

Consequently, the panel does not believe the claimant's allegations that her ex-spouse intends to go to El Salvador to threaten or to kill her, particularly since she stated that he is living in Montréal with another [translation] "girlfriend".
The panel concludes that the claimant is not credible regarding the alleged threats that she might experience in El Salvador from her former spouse, who lives in Canada.

However, although the panel does not believe that the claimant would be threatened because of her gender should she return to El Salvador, the panel does consider that, given the claimant's young age, the fact that she has spent eight years outside El Salvador, that she has already lived in Canada for five years, and that she has a son in Canada, the panel understands that she would want to improve her situation and remain in Canada. However, despite the sympathy that the panel feels toward this claimant, it does not have the jurisdiction to grant her refugee protection status on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

Having analyzed all of the evidence, the panel concludes that the claimant did not demonstrate that she faces a "serious possibility" of persecution under one of the Convention grounds, that is, as a member of a particular social group-women-should she return to El Salvador. She also did not demonstrate that, on a balance of probabilities, should she return to El Salvador, she would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or to a risk to her life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

Consequently, her claim for refugee protection is rejected.
